Our Story
Why engineering first is a business model, not a slogan.
Most telecom hardware companies start with a product catalogue and work backwards to a story. Saga started differently: with a thesis about what clients in this market actually need, and why most vendors aren't able to deliver it.
The thesis is straightforward. Enterprise and carrier-edge switch buyers don't just need a box that passes traffic. They need a platform they can build on — firmware they can customize, a supply chain they can rely on when allocation gets tight, and a technical relationship that doesn't reset every time they launch a new product generation.
"We're not a marketing-driven company. We put resources into engineering and inventory because that's where we actually create value for clients."
That means we focus on two chipset ecosystems — Marvell Prestera for access-layer switching, CENTEC for aggregation, core, and data center — and we go deep on both. We optimize feature sets continuously. We hold strategic buffer stock on key chipsets. We do firmware and management UI customization at a depth most suppliers won't touch.
The trade-off is transparency: we don't compete on every deal, and we're not the right partner for every buyer. We work best with clients who are optimizing for total cost of deployment, architectural consistency, and long-term supply predictability — not whoever quotes the lowest unit price this quarter.
Saga is based in Shenzhen. We work with OEM and ODM clients, system integrators, ISPs, and distributors across global markets. Our relationships are built to last, and we take the long view on every account we pursue.

Insights
Engineering perspectives on telecom procurement and supply chain.
August 2026 · Supply Chain
Why Strategic Inventory Matters in Telecom Procurement
+
For most procurement teams, the evaluation ends at unit price and lead time. But in telecom hardware — especially at the access and aggregation layer — there's a third variable that rarely appears on the RFQ: supply continuity risk.
Chipset allocation is not linear. Marvell and CENTEC silicon, like most semiconductors, moves in cycles. During tight allocation periods, factories that don't hold buffer stock simply can't ship — regardless of how good the unit price was when you signed the PO. The cost of a delayed network rollout, a stalled OEM product launch, or a missed project deadline dwarfs any savings made at the per-unit level.
Strategic inventory isn't speculative stockpiling. It's planned buffer stock held against specific chipsets, sized against client demand forecasts and the lifecycle position of each platform.
At Saga Telecom, we maintain buffer positions on key Marvell Prestera and CENTEC chipsets as a deliberate business decision — not as a side effect of over-ordering. This means predictable lead times for standard configurations, even during periods when the broader market is constrained.
Total cost of ownership in networking hardware is rarely about the switch itself. It's about deployment friction, supply predictability, and the cost of exceptions. A vendor who quotes 10% lower but delivers 6 weeks late — or can't fulfill at all during a shortage — is not a lower-cost option. The math doesn't work.
Before your next RFQ cycle, it's worth asking: does your supplier hold chipset-level buffer stock, or are they building to order against spot allocation? The answer tells you a lot about what happens when the market tightens — and it always tightens eventually.
August 2026 · Technology
Marvell vs. Generic Access Layer Switches — What Procurement Teams Miss
+
Access layer switching is often treated as a commodity purchase. The logic is straightforward: a 24-port managed switch is a 24-port managed switch. Standardize on price, move on. This logic breaks down in practice — usually at the worst possible moment.
Not all managed switches are built on the same silicon. The chipset underneath determines what the switch can actually do — not just today, but across its entire operational life. Generic and white-label switches frequently use silicon with limited feature roadmaps, minimal vendor support, and firmware that receives infrequent updates if any.
Marvell Prestera-based switches operate differently. The platform has active R&D investment behind it, a defined feature roadmap, and a support ecosystem that extends from the chip level through to firmware and management interfaces. When you deploy a Marvell-based switch, you're not buying a frozen feature set — you're buying into a platform that continues to develop.
Generic switches frequently support features on paper but implement them inconsistently — with firmware bugs that never get patched, or CLI behavior that doesn't match documentation.
For OEM and ODM buyers, the gap widens further. Generic silicon offers limited customization depth — surface-level rebranding at best. Marvell Prestera platforms support deep firmware customization: feature set activation, CLI behavior modification, SNMP and MIB configuration, and full management UI white-labeling.
When evaluating access layer options, the right question isn't "what does this switch support?" It's "what does the chipset platform allow, and who is maintaining it?" The answer determines not just what you can deploy today, but what you can build on for the next five years.
August 2026 · Procurement
How to Evaluate a Managed Switch Supplier Beyond Unit Price
+
The RFQ process optimizes for the wrong variable. Unit price is easy to compare — it fits neatly into a spreadsheet column, it responds to negotiation, and it produces a clear winner. The problem is that unit price is rarely where procurement decisions actually go wrong.
The real cost shows up later: in delayed shipments when a supplier can't fulfill during a shortage, in deployment friction when firmware doesn't behave as documented, in re-qualification costs when a chipset platform reaches end-of-life. None of these costs appear on the original RFQ.
Supply chain depth is the first non-price variable that matters.
Ask your supplier directly: do you hold chipset-level buffer stock, or do you build to order against spot allocation? A supplier who can't answer this question clearly doesn't have a strategic inventory position.
Technical support quality is the second.
Platform-level support means someone who understands CLI behavior, MIB implementation, and firmware interaction with your specific topology. Product-level support means someone who reads the datasheet back to you. The difference becomes obvious the first time you hit an edge case in production.
Chipset continuity is the third.
A supplier who carries products across multiple unrelated chipset platforms is optimizing for catalogue breadth, not technical depth. Ask which chipset families your supplier is committed to, and what their policy is on lifecycle management when a platform approaches EOL.
The quality of the answer to "what happens when allocation gets tight?" tells you more about a supplier than any price sheet.
August 2026 · OEM / ODM
OEM vs ODM vs SKD vs CKD — What the Differences Mean for Your Product Roadmap
+
These four terms appear on supplier capability sheets constantly, and they're often used interchangeably in ways that obscure meaningful differences. For buyers planning a hardware product roadmap, the distinctions matter — they determine how much control you have, how much risk you carry, and what your unit economics look like.
OEM — Original Equipment Manufacturing
You take an existing hardware design and apply your brand. Lowest friction to market, but your ability to differentiate on hardware is limited — your product looks like everyone else's under the skin.
ODM — Original Design Manufacturing
The manufacturer builds to your specification. You own the design output. This gives you meaningful hardware differentiation — port configurations, form factors, and performance profiles that are yours rather than shared across multiple brands.
SKD / CKD — Semi or Completely Knocked Down
Assembly models driven primarily by import duty optimization or local content requirements. SKD delivers major subassemblies; CKD delivers all components for full local assembly. Both require local assembly capability but can materially improve landed cost in the right market context.
Not all suppliers support all four models — and among those who do, capability depth varies significantly. Deep ODM means firmware and UI customization, not just PCB layout changes.
Most buyers start with OEM for speed to market and move toward ODM as volume and differentiation requirements grow. The question worth asking any supplier: how deep does the customization actually go?
September 2026 · Technology
When to Choose Industrial vs. Commercial Ethernet Switches — A Deployment Decision Framework
+
The question comes up on almost every project that involves networking hardware outside a standard office or data center environment: does this deployment actually need industrial-grade switches, or will commercial-grade hardware do the job?
The answer is not always obvious, and getting it wrong in either direction is expensive. Over-specifying adds cost without adding value. Under-specifying creates failures that are far more expensive to remediate than the equipment savings were worth.
This framework covers the four variables that should drive the decision.
Operating temperature range
Commercial Ethernet switches are typically rated for 0°C to 50°C — the standard range for climate-controlled environments. Industrial switches extend this to -40°C to +75°C, and some models go further.
The practical question is not what temperature the environment averages, but what it reaches at extremes. Outdoor cabinets in northern climates can hit -30°C in winter. Electrical substations and factory floors can exceed 60°C in summer without dedicated cooling. A commercial switch operating outside its rated range will not fail immediately — it will fail unpredictably, often under load, often at the worst possible time.
If your deployment includes outdoor enclosures, unheated industrial buildings, transportation infrastructure, or any environment without active climate control, the temperature specification is not optional.
Power supply architecture
Commercial switches ship with a single internal power supply. Industrial switches offer dual redundant inputs — either dual DC or AC/DC combinations — with hot-swap capability on higher-end models.
The relevant question here is what happens when power fails. For a commercial office deployment, a switch going down for 30 minutes while a PSU is replaced is an inconvenience. For a water treatment facility, a manufacturing line, a traffic management system, or a hospital network, the same 30 minutes has a real dollar or safety cost attached to it.
Dual PSU is not a luxury specification for these environments. It is the minimum viable reliability architecture.
Installation form factor
Commercial switches are rack-mount, designed for structured cabling rooms and data closets. Industrial switches are available in DIN-rail form factors, designed for mounting inside electrical panels and control cabinets where rack space doesn’t exist.
This is often the decision point that gets overlooked in the planning phase. A project that specifies commercial switches discovers midway through installation that the field cabinets have no rack space. DIN-rail mounting is not interchangeable with rack mounting — the enclosures, the cable management, and the power wiring are all different.
If your network nodes live inside control panels, junction boxes, or roadside cabinets, the form factor decision is made for you.
MTBF and certification requirements
Industrial switches are designed and tested to higher MTBF targets — typically 200,000 hours or more versus 50,000–100,000 hours for commercial-grade hardware. They also carry certifications relevant to specific industrial environments: EMC immunity, surge protection ratings (typically 4KV–6KV), and in some cases certifications for rail, maritime, or hazardous location applications.
For deployments in electrically noisy environments — near heavy motors, variable frequency drives, welding equipment, or high-voltage switching — the surge and EMC specifications matter. Commercial switches are not tested for these environments and will experience premature failures in them.
The decision framework
Use commercial-grade switching when: the deployment is inside a climate-controlled building, power redundancy is not a reliability requirement, rack mounting is available, and the electrical environment is clean.
Use industrial-grade switching when: any of the following apply — outdoor or uncontrolled temperature environment, power redundancy is required, DIN-rail installation is needed, or the electrical environment includes significant noise or surge risk.
The mistake worth avoiding is making this decision on budget alone. The cost difference between commercial and industrial hardware at the switch level is typically 20–40%. The cost of a field failure — equipment replacement, site visit, downtime, and the downstream consequences — is almost always larger.
September 2026 · Technology
PoE Budget Planning: The Calculation Most Network Engineers Get Wrong
+
PoE switches are sold with a total power budget number: 370W, 520W, 740W. Most deployments treat this number as the limit they’re working within. The problem is that the nameplate budget and the power actually available to connected devices are not the same number — and the gap is large enough to cause deployment failures.
Where the power goes
A PoE switch draws power from its power supply and uses it for two things: running the switch itself, and delivering power to connected PDs (powered devices). The switch’s own consumption — processors, memory, fans, uplink ports — comes out of the power supply budget before any PoE delivery happens.
A 370W switch might consume 30–50W for its own operation, leaving 320–340W for PoE delivery. This is not hidden information, but it is frequently not factored into deployment calculations that simply divide the nameplate budget by the number of ports.
Per-port maximums and how they interact
IEEE 802.3af delivers up to 15.4W per port. 802.3at delivers up to 30W. 802.3bt delivers up to 90W. These are the standards, but the actual power delivered to a device — the power at the PD, not at the PSE — is lower after cable loss. A device rated for 25.5W consumption may require 30W from the switch port to actually receive 25.5W after the cable.
This means sizing based on device consumption ratings rather than port delivery maximums will produce an undersized budget.
The calculation that fails
The common approach: take the number of cameras (or APs, or VoIP phones), multiply by their rated power consumption, check that it’s under the switch budget. This fails because: it uses device consumption rather than port delivery requirements. It doesn’t account for switch self-consumption. It assumes all ports will never simultaneously draw maximum power — which is fine for diverse mixed deployments but wrong for uniform high-power deployments. And it doesn’t include headroom for power spikes during device startup, which can be 20–30% above steady-state draw.
The calculation that works
Start with the switch’s actual PoE delivery capacity — typically 85–90% of nameplate budget after self-consumption. For each port, use the IEEE maximum for that port’s standard, not the device’s rated consumption. Sum the per-port maximums for all ports you intend to actively use. Add 20% headroom for startup peaks and future capacity. If the result exceeds the switch’s PoE delivery capacity, the switch is undersized for this deployment.
For a 48-port deployment with 802.3at cameras averaging 15W consumption: the correct sizing assumes 30W per port delivery requirement, 48 ports × 30W = 1440W delivery requirement. A 740W switch delivers approximately 650–680W after self-consumption. This deployment needs either two switches or a higher-budget single switch — not a 740W unit.
The budget number to ask for
When evaluating switches, ask for the PoE delivery budget, not the total power budget.
These are different numbers, and suppliers who can’t distinguish between them are not the right partners for a deployment where PoE reliability matters.
The calculation is not complicated. The failure mode is treating it as simpler than it is.
October 2026 · Supply Chain
What Happens to Your Project When Chipset Allocation Tightens — A Real Scenario
+
This is not a theoretical risk. It has happened repeatedly — in 2020, 2021, 2022, and in smaller cycles since. The pattern is consistent enough that it is worth walking through what actually occurs at the project level when chipset allocation tightens, so that procurement teams can assess their own exposure before the next cycle hits.
The scenario
A system integrator wins a contract to deploy 200 access-layer switches across a campus network expansion. The project timeline is 14 weeks from PO to final acceptance. The switches are specified, the vendor is selected, the price is agreed. The order is placed.
Six weeks later, the vendor’s factory informs them that the Ethernet switch chipset they use — the same chipset that has been available with 4-week lead times for the past two years — is now on allocation. Allocation means the chipset manufacturer has capped how many units each customer can receive per quarter. The vendor’s allocation is enough to cover roughly 40% of the order.
The vendor has three options: ship partial, source alternative chipsets, or delay. Partial shipment pushes the project into a staged deployment the customer didn’t plan for. Alternative chipsets mean different firmware, different CLI behavior, potentially different feature sets — a re-qualification process that takes weeks the project doesn’t have. Delay means the contractor misses the acceptance deadline.
Where the failure actually occurs
The failure is not the shortage itself. The failure is the assumption that current lead times represent structural availability.
Semiconductor cycles are predictable at the macro level even when the timing is uncertain.
Suppliers who build to order against spot chipset allocation — placing their component orders only after customer POs are received — have zero buffer between market tightness and delivery failure. When allocation caps hit, these suppliers have no inventory to draw from. Every project in their queue is affected simultaneously.
What buffer stock actually means in practice
A supplier who holds strategic chipset inventory has pre-purchased components against demand forecasts. When allocation tightens, they are drawing from stock they already own rather than competing for new allocation on a constrained market.
This does not make them immune to extended shortages. But it means the gap between “allocation tightens” and “delivery failure” is measured in months rather than days. For a 14-week project, the difference between a supplier with 10 weeks of buffer stock and one with zero buffer stock is the difference between delivery and failure.
The question to add to supplier qualification
Before the next project, ask your switch supplier directly: what is your current chipset inventory position for the models I’m specifying? How many units do you have on hand today, and how many weeks of demand does that represent at your current run rate?
A supplier who can answer this question specifically — with numbers — has a strategic inventory position. A supplier who responds with lead time estimates and assurances about their “strong supplier relationships” does not.
The answer to this question is more predictive of project delivery reliability than any other variable in the vendor selection process.
October 2026 · OEM / ODM
Five Questions to Ask Before Signing an OEM Switch Agreement
+
OEM switch agreements are not all equivalent. The contract terms, the supplier relationship, and the technical depth behind the customization capability vary enormously between suppliers who describe themselves using the same language. These five questions separate suppliers who can actually deliver on OEM commitments from those who are rebranding catalogue products with a label change and calling it OEM.
1. Who owns the firmware roadmap, and what is your update cadence?
This is the most consequential question for long-cycle OEM products. If you are building a product line that will be in market for three to five years, the firmware it ships with at launch will need to be updated — for bug fixes, security patches, feature additions, and compatibility with evolving network environments.
Ask specifically: does the supplier maintain their own firmware development capability, or are they dependent on the chipset manufacturer’s reference firmware? What is the release cadence for firmware updates? What is the process for requesting firmware changes specific to your product?
A supplier who cannot answer these questions is not an OEM partner — they are a product reseller with your logo on it.
2. What is your EOL (end-of-life) policy for chipsets and products?
Chipset platforms have defined lifecycles. When the underlying silicon reaches end-of-life, the supplier must either migrate to a new platform or stop production. For OEM buyers, a chipset EOL event can force a complete product re-spin, including regulatory re-certification, firmware re-qualification, and supply chain transition.
Ask for the supplier’s policy in writing: how far in advance will you notify us of chipset EOL? What migration path will you support? Will you maintain production capability for existing designs for a defined period after EOL announcement?
A supplier who has never thought about this question cannot be relied upon for long-cycle product programs.
3. How deep does firmware customization actually go?
OEM firmware customization ranges from changing the login banner to rewriting the management interface, modifying CLI command structure, activating or deactivating feature sets, and altering MIB definitions. These are not equivalent capabilities.
Ask for specific examples: can you change the CLI prompt and command set? Can you disable features that should not be accessible to end users? Can you modify the SNMP MIB to expose custom OIDs? Can you change the web management interface beyond branding?
Request a demonstration on a reference platform. The answer to “yes, we support firmware customization” should include a list of specific things that have been done for other customers, not a general capability statement.
4. What is your chipset inventory position, and how do you protect long-term supply?
OEM programs typically involve volume commitments over multi-year periods. A supplier who cannot guarantee component availability across the program duration is transferring supply chain risk onto you — the OEM buyer — without disclosing it.
Ask: do you hold strategic buffer stock on the chipsets used in my product? What is your current inventory position? What happens to my production schedule if chipset allocation tightens? Do you have a secondary source for critical components?
The difference between a supplier with strategic inventory and one without it becomes visible the first time a shortage hits. By then, it is too late to change suppliers without a gap in your production.
5. What does your QC process look like before units ship?
OEM products carry your brand. Field failures are your warranty exposure and your customer relationship problem, regardless of which factory produced the hardware. Understanding the supplier’s quality control process before you sign is not optional.
Ask for the QC checklist: what tests does every unit go through before it leaves the factory? Is there incoming inspection of chipsets and key components? What is the failure rate at final test? What happens to units that fail — are they repaired and retested, or scrapped?
A supplier who cannot produce a written QC procedure does not have one. A supplier who has never been asked this question by a customer is not an OEM supplier in any meaningful sense of the term.
Using these questions
The value of asking these questions is not primarily in the answers — it is in the quality of how the supplier engages with them. A supplier who has a strategic inventory position, a firmware roadmap, and a written QC process will answer these questions specifically and confidently. A supplier who is operating as a product reseller will deflect, generalize, and change the subject.
The questions are a filter, not a checklist. Use them accordingly.

Ethernet Switching for CCTV and IP Surveillance: What Actually Matters
+
IP surveillance is one of the most common deployment contexts for access-layer Ethernet switching, and one of the most frequently misconfigured. The hardware decisions that determine whether a CCTV network performs reliably are not the same decisions that matter in a general enterprise network. This article covers what actually matters for surveillance deployments — and what is often over-specified or under-specified.
Bandwidth is the starting point, not the end point
The first calculation in any surveillance switch specification is bandwidth. A 4MP camera at H.264 compression generates approximately 4–8 Mbps of sustained traffic. A 4K camera at H.265 generates 8–20 Mbps depending on scene complexity and compression settings. Multiply by the number of cameras on each switch, add 20% headroom for motion events and stream peaks, and you have the minimum uplink bandwidth requirement.
For a 24-port switch serving 24 × 4MP cameras at 6 Mbps average: 144 Mbps sustained, 173 Mbps with headroom. A single 1G uplink handles this comfortably. For 24 × 4K cameras at 15 Mbps: 360 Mbps sustained, 432 Mbps with headroom. A single 1G uplink is marginal. Two 1G uplinks in LAG or a single 10G uplink is the correct specification.
This calculation is basic, but it is missed regularly when projects spec switches by port count rather than throughput.
IGMP snooping is not optional
IP cameras multicast their video streams by default in most configurations. Without IGMP snooping enabled and correctly configured, multicast traffic floods to every port on the switch — including ports not connected to any NVR or viewing station. On a 48-port switch with 48 cameras, this means every camera’s stream is sent to every other camera port, multiplying the effective traffic by 48 and saturating the switch fabric.
IGMP snooping constrains multicast delivery to only the ports where a listener has registered.
For surveillance networks with more than a handful of cameras, IGMP snooping is not a nice-to-have feature — it is the difference between a functional network and one that is saturated at modest camera counts.
Verify that IGMP snooping is supported, enabled by default or easy to enable, and that the switch supports IGMP v2 and v3. Also verify that the querier function is available — in networks without a dedicated multicast router, the switch needs to act as the IGMP querier or multicast group membership will time out.
PoE planning for surveillance
Most IP cameras are PoE-powered. The PoE budget calculation for a surveillance network follows the same principles as any PoE deployment, but with one surveillance-specific consideration: cameras draw more power in cold weather. A camera rated for 12W at 20°C may draw 15–18W at -10°C as the IR illuminators and heaters work harder.
For outdoor surveillance deployments, use the cold-weather power draw specification — not the nominal specification — when calculating PoE budgets. This number is not always published prominently. Ask for it specifically.
Also consider startup surge: PTZ cameras and cameras with IR illuminators draw significantly more power for 1–3 seconds at startup than at steady state. Switches with per-port PoE scheduling can stagger camera startup to prevent a simultaneous surge from tripping the PoE budget limit.
Ring topology and ERPS for resilience
Large surveillance networks — transportation, campus perimeter, industrial facilities — frequently use ring topologies to maximize fiber coverage while minimizing cable runs. A ring of switches connects cameras across a large physical area with a single fiber loop rather than a star topology that would require individual runs back to a central point.
Ring topologies require a loop protection protocol to prevent broadcast storms. STP/RSTP works but has convergence times of 1–30 seconds, during which video streams from cameras on the failed segment are lost. For surveillance applications where continuous recording is required, this is unacceptable.
ERPS G.8032 converges in under 20ms — imperceptible in a video stream. For any surveillance deployment using ring topology, ERPS is the correct choice. Verify that your switch supports ERPS and that it supports it in the version of firmware you will actually be deploying.
Storage network separation
NVRs writing surveillance footage generate sustained write traffic that competes with camera ingest traffic if both are on the same network segment. For deployments with more than a few cameras writing to a central NVR, separating camera traffic from NVR-to-storage traffic using VLANs reduces contention and simplifies QoS policy.
This is not a complex configuration, but it requires a managed switch with VLAN support — an obvious requirement that is occasionally forgotten when projects substitute unmanaged switches to save cost on camera-side ports.
The specification that is usually over-specified
Layer 3 routing is rarely needed at the access layer in a surveillance network. Most CCTV deployments route between the camera network and the management/viewing network at a single aggregation point — a router, a firewall, or an L3 aggregation switch. Access-layer switches in a surveillance network are almost always L2+ devices, and specifying L3 access switches for surveillance adds cost without adding capability.
The exception is very large distributed deployments where routing at the edge reduces traffic concentration. For standard deployments, L2+ with IGMP snooping, ERPS, and appropriate PoE budget covers all requirements.

Why Marvell Prestera Switches Work Better for Long-Cycle OEM Products
+
OEM hardware product lines have different requirements than one-time procurement decisions. When you are building a switch product that will be sold under your brand, supported by your technical team, and potentially in market for three to five years, the chipset platform underneath it matters in ways that are not visible in a spec sheet comparison. This is the case for choosing Marvell Prestera as the platform for long-cycle OEM switch products.
Platform continuity across product generations
A chipset platform is not just a component — it is a technical foundation that your firmware, your CLI documentation, your support team’s expertise, and your customers’ configurations are all built on top of.
When a chipset platform reaches end-of-life and a supplier migrates to a new platform, everything built on top of the old platform has to be rebuilt. Firmware is rewritten. CLI command structures change. MIB definitions shift. Features that existed on the old platform may not exist on the new one in the same form, or at all. Customers who have automated configurations, monitoring integrations, or scripts built around your product’s CLI behavior face unexpected changes.
Marvell Prestera is a mature, actively developed platform with a defined roadmap. The AC5 series — AC5 Lite, AC5, AC5+ — shares a common architecture and firmware foundation. Products built on AC5 Lite can be migrated to AC5 or AC5+ with firmware compatibility maintained across the platform family. This means a product line started on AC5 Lite can grow in capability without a platform re-spin.
Firmware depth and update cadence
For OEM products, firmware is not a background concern — it is part of the product. Your customers will expect firmware updates for security patches, bug fixes, and feature additions over the product’s commercial lifetime. The question is who maintains the firmware and how.
Marvell Prestera-based products benefit from active firmware development at the chipset level. New features introduced in updated firmware — protocol support additions, security enhancements, management capability improvements — flow through to switch products without requiring hardware changes. This means an OEM product built on Prestera today will have access to firmware improvements developed over the next several years on the same silicon.
The alternative — generic or white-label silicon with minimal vendor investment — delivers firmware that was complete at launch and receives minimal updates thereafter. For a product sold with a 3-year warranty and expected to be in service for 5 years, this is a significant liability.
Customization depth that holds across the product lifecycle
Deep OEM customization — firmware feature set configuration, CLI behavior modification, management UI white-labeling, MIB customization — requires detailed platform knowledge that takes years to develop. A supplier with genuine Marvell Prestera expertise can customize at the SDK level, not just at the configuration file level.
The practical difference is significant.
Configuration-level customization changes what is enabled or disabled on a fixed firmware. SDK-level customization changes how the platform behaves.
For OEM buyers who need their product to behave like their product — not like a generic switch with their logo — SDK-level customization is the requirement.
This level of customization is stable across the Prestera platform family. Customizations developed for one AC5-based product are portable across the platform, which means your second product generation does not require starting the customization process from scratch.
The lifecycle cost calculation
The per-unit cost difference between a Marvell Prestera-based switch and a generic-silicon alternative is typically 15–25% at equivalent port count and feature level. Over a product line lifetime, this difference needs to be weighed against:
Re-qualification costs when a generic platform reaches EOL — typically 3–6 months of engineering time plus regulatory recertification. Firmware maintenance costs for platform-specific issues that the chipset vendor does not address. Customer support costs for CLI inconsistencies and firmware bugs that do not get patched. Brand exposure from field failures caused by platform quality issues.
For single-project procurement where the switch is a line item rather than a product, the per-unit cost comparison is the right framework. For OEM product programs where the switch is the product, the lifecycle cost comparison is the right framework. They produce different answers.
What to verify with any Prestera-based supplier
Not every supplier who lists Marvell Prestera on their specification sheet has genuine platform depth. Verify specifically: do they have direct access to Marvell’s SDK? Can they demonstrate firmware customizations they have delivered for other OEM customers? Do they maintain a dedicated firmware engineering team, or do they depend entirely on the chipset manufacturer’s reference firmware?
The answers to these questions determine whether you are getting a genuine Marvell Prestera OEM partner or a supplier who happens to use Prestera silicon and is reselling reference designs with label changes.

The Hidden Cost of Switching Chipset Platforms Mid-Program
+
Every OEM hardware program eventually faces a chipset transition. The silicon that was available and cost-effective when the program started reaches end-of-life, or a new platform promises better performance at lower cost, or a supply disruption forces a re-evaluation. The transition looks straightforward on paper — new chipset, same form factor, updated firmware. In practice, the cost and timeline of a mid-program chipset transition is almost always underestimated, often significantly.
This is not an argument against ever changing platforms. It is an account of what the transition actually involves, so that the decision is made with accurate cost information rather than optimistic assumptions.
The firmware rewrite
Switching silicon vendors means switching SDKs. The software development kit that interfaces between the chipset hardware and the network operating system is vendor-specific and not portable. Every feature that was implemented against the previous SDK — VLAN handling, QoS policies, IGMP snooping behavior, ERPS ring protection, ACL processing — has to be re-implemented against the new SDK.
This is not a port. SDK APIs are not standardized across chipset vendors. The data structures are different, the event models are different, the hardware abstraction layers are different. Features that took weeks to develop and stabilize on the original platform can take equally long on the new one, and frequently reveal new edge cases and bugs that weren’t present on the mature original.
For a switch firmware with 18 months of development and stabilization behind it, a platform transition typically requires 6–12 months of firmware re-development before the new platform reaches equivalent feature parity and stability. During this period, the product is unavailable or in a degraded feature state.
Regulatory recertification
A chipset change is a significant hardware modification that triggers recertification requirements for CE, FCC, and other mandatory certifications. The new chipset has different emissions characteristics, different power consumption profiles, and potentially different radio frequency behavior from the original. Regulators treat it as a new product submission, not an update to an existing certification.
CE and FCC recertification timelines range from 8 to 20 weeks depending on the testing lab queue, the complexity of the product, and whether any issues are found during testing that require hardware modification before re-submission. This timeline runs in parallel with firmware development in the best case. In practice, it often cannot begin until the hardware is stable enough to submit for testing, which means it frequently extends the total transition timeline rather than compressing it.
UKCA, RoHS, and REACH documentation must also be updated to reflect the new component. For products sold into markets with additional country-specific certifications, each certification follows its own process.
Customer configuration compatibility
Your customers have deployed your product. They have configured it. They have written scripts, monitoring integrations, and automation against its CLI. They have saved configuration backups that they expect to be restorable on replacement units.
A chipset transition typically changes CLI behavior. Commands that existed on the original platform may not exist on the new one. Commands that exist on both may behave differently. Configuration syntax may change. MIB OIDs used for SNMP monitoring may shift.
For customers who have built operational tooling around your product’s CLI, a chipset transition is a migration project — one that you have effectively handed them without warning or budget. The support burden this generates, and the customer relationship cost, is rarely accounted for in the transition business case.
The inventory transition problem
You have existing inventory of the old product in your warehouse, in your channel, and in transit. You have customers with open orders. You have service contracts that specify the original model.
Managing the transition between old and new inventory — communicating EOL timelines, honoring existing orders, maintaining spare part availability for units already in the field, and handling customers who refuse to accept the new platform — is an operational project that runs for 12–24 months alongside the development and certification work.
What this means for platform selection
The cost of a chipset transition is highest when it is unplanned and forced — by EOL, by supply disruption, or by a supplier who did not invest in the original platform’s longevity. It is lower, but still significant, when it is planned and gradual.
The practical implication for OEM product planning is that platform selection is not just a cost-per-unit decision. The cost of the platform you are not on — the cost of transitioning away from a platform that reaches EOL prematurely, or that receives inadequate vendor investment — is a real cost that belongs in the selection analysis.
Choosing a chipset platform with active development, a defined multi-year roadmap, and a supplier who has invested in SDK-level expertise is not a premium. It is the lower-cost option when the full program lifecycle is the unit of analysis.

What “OEM/ODM Support” Actually Means — And How to Tell the Difference
+
OEM and ODM support are claimed by nearly every switch supplier in the market. The claim ranges from “we can put your logo on the front panel” to “we will develop firmware to your specification, certify the product under your brand, and support it through its commercial lifecycle.” These are not the same capability, and the label does not distinguish between them.
This article describes what genuine OEM and ODM support looks like at each level of customization, and what questions surface the difference between suppliers who can deliver it and those who cannot.
Level 1: Branding only
The most common interpretation of OEM support is cosmetic: your logo replaces the manufacturer’s logo on the front panel, the packaging carries your brand, and the documentation uses your product name. The firmware is unchanged. The CLI prompt says your company name. The web management interface may have your logo in the header.
This is widely available and technically straightforward. It requires no SDK access and no firmware development capability. Most Shenzhen-based switch manufacturers can do this.
What it does not give you: any differentiation in behavior, any ability to restrict or modify feature sets, any control over CLI structure, any integration with your own management systems at a protocol level. Your branded product is the manufacturer’s product with a different label. Any other supplier using the same platform can produce an identical product.
Level 2: Feature set configuration
The next level involves configuring which features are enabled or visible on the platform — without modifying how they work. A supplier with good platform knowledge can enable or disable features in the factory image, configure default settings, set default VLAN assignments, and determine which CLI commands and web interface sections are exposed to end users.
This level requires access to the platform’s configuration layer and familiarity with its option space. It is more meaningful than branding-only OEM but still does not involve development — it involves configuration of an existing system.
What it gives you: a product that behaves differently from the manufacturer’s standard offering out of the box. A simplified interface for customers who don’t need advanced features. Default configurations that match your deployment standards.
What it does not give you: the ability to add new features, change how existing features behave at a protocol level, or modify the management interface in structural ways.
Level 3: Firmware development
Genuine ODM capability at the firmware level means the supplier has SDK access and development capability against the chipset’s software development kit. They can implement new features, modify existing feature behavior, change CLI command structure, add custom CLI commands, modify SNMP MIB definitions, and change how the switch interacts with external management systems.
This is where the meaningful differentiation happens. A product developed at the firmware level can have genuinely different behavior from any other product on the same silicon — different CLI, different management interface, different protocol behavior, different integration points.
This requires years of platform investment. SDK development is not something a supplier picks up for a single customer program. The suppliers who have it have been investing in it for multiple years, typically across multiple customer programs.
How to verify: ask for specific examples. What features have you implemented that are not in the chipset manufacturer’s reference firmware? What CLI commands exist in your firmware that do not exist in standard firmware? Can you demonstrate a management UI that is structurally different from the reference design? The answers should be specific and demonstrable, not descriptive.
Level 4: Hardware and mechanical customization
Full ODM extends to hardware design — port count and configuration, chassis form factor, power supply specification, front and rear panel layout, LED configuration, and mechanical dimensions. This level requires the supplier to have hardware design capability beyond assembling reference board designs.
Not all suppliers who claim ODM support operate at this level. For most OEM programs, Level 3 firmware customization combined with mechanical branding covers the requirement. Hardware-level ODM is relevant when your product specification diverges significantly from available reference designs — unusual port configurations, specific form factor requirements, or integration of non-standard hardware components.
The question that reveals the level
A single question surfaces where a supplier’s OEM/ODM capability actually sits: “Can you show me a product you have delivered for another OEM customer that has different CLI behavior from your standard firmware?”
If the answer is yes and they can demonstrate it, the supplier has Level 3 capability. If the answer involves showing you a rebranded product with the same CLI as their standard offering, the supplier is operating at Level 1 or 2. If the answer is vague or deflects to production capability and quality, the supplier has not delivered genuine firmware-level ODM.
Matching your requirement to the right level
Not every OEM program needs Level 3. If you need a product with your brand, a simplified interface, and default configurations that match your deployment standards, Level 2 is sufficient and available from a wide range of suppliers.
If you need a product that behaves like your product — with CLI behavior, management interfaces, and protocol implementations that are specific to your requirements and not replicable by a competitor buying from the same manufacturer — Level 3 is the requirement, and the supplier pool is significantly smaller.
Knowing which level you need before entering supplier discussions determines whether you are evaluating the right suppliers with the right questions.
